MD simulations workflow

Preparing and running MD simulation for a protein-ligand complex involves several key steps from system preparation to MD trajectory production.

System preparation

Each system is meticulously prepared to conform to the requirements of the selected force field. The nomenclature of atomic types and residue names is force field-specific, typically differing from that of the PDB. Notably, force fields exhibit distinctions in the protonation states of histidine, which are not explicitly captured in the PDB format. These states include charged state, neutral τ tautomer, anionic τ tautomer, and anionic π tautomer. Subsequently, any missing hydrogens are systematically added, and the hydrogen bonding network undergoes optimization. This optimization involves the rotation of the side chains of asparagine, glutamine, and histidine residues, or the adjustment of the protonation state in the case of histidines [114].

System solvation

Each protein-ligand complex is placed within a water box, which may take the form of a cubic, rectangular, triclinic, or orthorhombic shape. This configuration ensures a minimum water layer of at least 10 Å surrounds the complex. The choice of a water model, such as Single Point Charge (SPC) or Transferable Intermolecular Potential 3 Point (TIP3P), is crucial for accurately representing the behavior of water molecules in the simulation.

System neutralization

Additionally, the overall charge of the complex must be neutralized, this is achieved by adding Na+ and Cl− ions to the solvent. The electrostatic potential is computed at multiple points on a grid that spans the volume of the system, accounting for the positions of ions.

Energy minimization

The energy minimization step aims to optimize the molecular structure and reach a more stable starting configuration. It relieves steric clashes, corrects bond distortions, and allows the system to settle into a local energy minimum. During this step, an iterative optimization algorithm like steepest descent or conjugate gradient is used to adjust the atomic coordinates and minimize the potential energy of the system. Forces on atoms are calculated and positions are adjusted in each iteration until convergence criteria like an energy threshold or maximum iterations are met. The goal is to guide the system to a local minimum on the potential energy surface, where forces on each atom are near zero. After minimization, the stability and quality of the minimized structure are assessed by checking bond parameters, examining the overall structure, and ensuring no major clashes or unrealistic distortions remain. This step is crucial for obtaining a reasonable starting point for further calculations or simulations.

Equilibration

Following energy minimization, the equilibration step involves adjusting the system’s temperature and pressure, allowing solvent molecules to properly interact with the biomolecular components.

  • NVT Equilibration (Constant Number of Particles, Volume, and Temperature): In the first equilibration phase, the system is allowed to evolve at a constant temperature (NVT ensemble). This involves applying a thermostat to control the temperature and adjusting atomic velocities accordingly. The duration of this phase allows the system to reach a thermal equilibrium, where the temperature fluctuations stabilize.
  • NPT Equilibration (Constant Number of Particles, Pressure, and Temperature): Subsequently, the system undergoes equilibration at a constant temperature and pressure (NPT ensemble). This phase includes the application of a barostat to control pressure and may involve adjusting box dimensions to achieve the desired pressure. The system is allowed to equilibrate under these conditions, ensuring that both temperature and pressure fluctuations reach a stable state.
Production MD

Following NVT and NPT equilibration, the system transitions to the production MD run, where the dynamics of the protein-ligand complex are observed over an extended period. This phase is critical for obtaining meaningful data on the system’s behavior.

MD trajectory data analysis

In the analysis phase of the MD simulation, various techniques are employed to extract meaningful insights from the obtained trajectory data.

Root-Mean-Square Deviation

The Root-Mean-Square Deviation (RMSD) is a measure of the similarity between two structures. The RMSD between two structures $v$ and $w$ of $n$ atoms each (or $n$ points) is calculated with the following formula (Eq. 15):

$$ \text{RMSD}_{v,w} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\left\| v_{i} - w_{i} \right\|^{2}} \tag{15} $$

RMSD is used to compare protein structures. It is typically applied to the Cα atoms of the protein. In MD analysis, it is used to observe the deviation of the system from the initial structure. The system is equilibrated when the RMSD reaches a plateau. Other analyses are typically performed on the stabilized portion of the trajectory.

Root-Mean-Square Fluctuation

While RMSD is an average calculated over all atomic coordinates of the system at each step of the trajectory. The Root-Mean-Square Fluctuation (RMSF) corresponds to an average calculated over all steps of the trajectory for each atom (Eq. 16).

$$ \text{RMSF}_{i} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t = 0}^{t = T}\left( x_{i}^{t} - {x\bar{}}_{i} \right)^{2}} \tag{16} $$

Here, $\text{RMSF}_{i}$represents the fluctuation of atom $i$ calculated over a trajectory of $T$ steps. It is determined by taking the square root of the average squared distance between the position of the atom at time t$(x_{i}^{t}$) and the average position of the atom (${x\bar{}}_{i}$). This analysis provides valuable insights into stable regions within protein structures.

Radius of gyration

The radius of gyration (Rg) is a measure of the compactness or spread of a molecular structure around its center of mass. Changes in Rag may indicate structural transitions, such as protein folding/unfolding or conformational changes induced by ligand binding or unbinding. Mathematically, the Rg can be expressed as (Eq. 17):

$$ Rg = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i = 1}^{N}{m_{i}r_{i}^{2}}} \tag{17} $$

Where $N$ is the total number of atoms, $m_{i}$is the mass of atom $i$, $r_{i}$ is the distance of atom $i$ from the centre of mass.

Solvent-accessible surface area

Solvent Accessible Surface Area (SASA) provides insights into the accessibility of a protein’s surface to its surrounding solvent environment. SASA quantifies the extent to which atoms on the protein surface are accessible to solvent molecules, influencing various biological processes, including ligand binding. Changes in SASA during protein-ligand interactions can indicate alterations in the protein’s conformation, accessibility of binding sites, and the potential impact on ligand binding affinity.

The Shrake-Rupley algorithm is widely employed for SASA calculations due to its computational efficiency. It involves rolling a probe sphere over the molecular surface and determining the solvent-accessible points, allowing for an estimation of the accessible surface area of the biomolecule.

Hydrogen bond analysis

Hydrogen bonds play a crucial role in maintaining the structure of proteins. The energy required to break a hydrogen bond ranges from 5 to 30 kJ/mol, making it stronger than van der Waals interactions but weaker than ionic or covalent bonds. Hydrogen bonds involve an electronegative atom such as oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine, and a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to another electronegative atom.

The formation of a hydrogen bond depends on the relative position and the types of atoms in the donor (D) and acceptor (A). In MD simulations, observations on hydrogen bonds include the average number of bonds, which can be used to compare interactions between atom groups, and an analysis of occupancy or presence, providing information on stable regions within a molecule. Parameters such as the angle (θ) between the DH and DA vectors and the distance (d) between D and A are crucial, with θ being less than 40° and d less than 3.5 Å for effective hydrogen bonding as illustrated in Figure 19 [115].

Principal component analysis

Principal component analysis (PCA) is a powerful statistical method that aims to reduce the dimensionality of a dataset while retaining the essential features and variability present in the original data. In the context of MD simulations of biomolecular systems, PCA is particularly valuable for identifying dominant motions, describing structural variations, and uncovering the principal components governing the system’s dynamics.

  • Covariance Matrix: PCA begins by constructing the covariance matrix from the atomic positional fluctuations obtained during the MD simulation.

  • Eigen decomposition: The covariance matrix is then diagonalized, yielding eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

  • Principal Components: The eigenvectors represent the principal components, and the eigenvalues indicate the magnitude of the variance along each principal component.

Free energy calculations

Molecular mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area

Molecular mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area (MM/GBSA) is a computational approach used to estimate free energy changes in biomolecular systems, particularly for studying binding affinities of ligands to proteins [116]. The MM/GBSA method was developed by Peter Kollman and his group at the University of California, San Diego (UCSD) in the late 1990s [117]. It combines MM calculations, which describe the bonded and non-bonded interactions within the system, with a continuum solvation model based on the Generalized Born (GB) theory to account for solvent effects [118]. The binding free energy of a ligand to a protein receptor is calculated as the thermodynamic difference between the individual free energies of the free protein (P), the free ligand (L), and the formed complex (PL) in solvent (Eq. 18):

$$ \text{ΔG}_{\text{bind}} = G_{\text{PL}} - (G_{P} + G_{L}) \tag{18} $$

The binding free energy can be decomposed into the vacuum potential energy, $\text{ΔE}_{\text{MM}}$, which includes the energy of both bonded as well as non-bonded interactions (Eq. 19), and it is calculated based on the MM force-field parameters [119,120].

$$ \text{ΔE}_{\text{MM}} = \text{ΔE}_{\text{bonded}} + \text{ΔE}_{\text{nonbonded}} = \text{ΔE}_{\text{bonded}} + ( \text{ΔE}_{\text{ele}} + \text{ΔE}_{\text{vdw}}) \tag{19} $$

Where $\text{ΔE}_{\text{bonded}}$represents bonded interactions encompassing bond, angle, dihedral, and improper interactions. $\text{ΔE}_{\text{nonbonded}}$ represents nonbonded interactions comprising both electrostatic ($\text{ΔE}_{\text{ele}}$) and van der Waals ($\text{ΔE}_{\text{vdw}}$) interactions, modeled through Coulomb and Lennard-Jones potential functions, respectively. In the single trajectory approach, the conformation of the protein and ligand in both the bound and unbound forms is assumed to be identical. Consequently, $\text{ΔE}_{\text{bonded}}$is consistently considered as zero [121].

This binding free energy can be further described to account for the free energy of solvation (Eq. 20):

$$ \text{ΔG}_{\text{bind}} = \text{ΔE}_{\text{ele}} + \text{ΔE}_{\text{vdw}} + \text{ΔG}_{\text{GB}} + \text{ΔG}_{\text{SASA}} - T\Delta S \tag{20} $$

The equation incorporates the solvation energy ($\text{ΔG}_{\text{GB}}$) accounting for polar solvation effects using an implicit solvation GB model, and the SASA solvation energy ($\text{ΔG}_{\text{SASA}}$) capturing nonpolar solvation effects based on the approximation of SASA [122]. The conformational entropy term ($- T\Delta S$) which is calculated by normal-mode analysis, is usually neglected due to the high computational cost and technical errors associated with its calculation [123].

Molecular mechanics/Poisson-Boltzmann Surface Area

Like MM/GBSA, Molecular mechanics/Poisson-Boltzmann Surface Area (MM/PBSA) is a computational method used for the estimation of free energy changes in biomolecular systems, especially for studying ligand binding to proteins. MM/PBSA combines MM calculations with a continuum solvation model as described in MM/GBSA (Eq. 21), but it uses the computationally time-consuming Poisson-Boltzmann (PB) equation to describe the electrostatic solvation effects ($\text{ΔG}_{\text{solv}})$ [124].

$$ \text{ΔG}_{\text{bind}} = \text{ΔE}_{\text{ele}} + \text{ΔE}_{\text{vdw}} + \text{ΔG}_{\text{solv}} + \text{ΔG}_{\text{SASA}} - T\Delta S \tag{21} $$

MD simulations software

There are several software packages available for MD simulations. Some popular options include GROMACS, AMBER, Desmond, LAMMPS, and NAMD. These software packages are widely used for MD simulations and offer various features suitable for different research needs. GROMACS is a free and open-source software suite for high-performance MD and output analysis [125], while AMBER is a suite of programs for MD simulations of proteins and nucleic acids [126]. Desmond is a high-performance MD simulation software package developed at D. E. Shaw Research. It is designed to perform MD simulations of biological systems on conventional computer clusters and can also be used for absolute and relative free energy calculations, such as free energy perturbation [127]. LAMMPS is a classical MD code with a focus on materials modelling [128]. NAMD is a powerful, parallel MD simulation software package [129]. Conclusion

Cheminformatics and computational methods have become indispensable in modern drug discovery, significantly accelerating the identification and optimization of drug candidates while reducing costs and experimental failures. This review highlights the transformative impact of key methodologies such as QSAR modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and ligand- and structure-based virtual screening. The integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning further enhances the predictive power and efficiency of these approaches, enabling the analysis of large datasets and uncovering complex structure-activity relationships.

Advancements in cheminformatics tools, molecular representations, and bioactivity databases have expanded the scope and depth of drug discovery pipelines. Moreover, the incorporation of ADMET profiling at early stages provides a more holistic evaluation of drug-likeness, optimizing the likelihood of clinical success. While these computational techniques offer immense potential, challenges such as data standardization, model validation, and limited interpretability of machine learning models persist.

Future efforts should focus on improving the integration of computational methods with experimental workflows, leveraging next-generation technologies like quantum computing and generative AI for de novo drug design. By addressing existing challenges and harnessing the synergy between computational and experimental approaches, researchers can continue to advance the development of safe, effective, and innovative therapeutics, ultimately transforming healthcare outcomes globally.

item.title: What Agentic Engineering Means for Computational Drug Discovery
item.description:
Simon Willison’s late-2025 claim, from and his , is that agentic coding crossed from “watch it” to “it usually does the thing.” Read that through a docking or MD project and the scarce resource is unchanged. It is still knowing whether the result is the science you asked for.

What got cheaper

For an MD analysis script, a virtual screen, or a substrate classifier, the new fact is reliability rather than a demo that sometimes runs. The code is scaffolding. The science is whether the pose is the right pose, whether the model holds across CYP isoforms, and whether a geometric feature is the feature you think it is. An agent that can build the scaffolding moves time onto the ensemble, the score, and that feature.

Validation was already the slow step

Implementation is no longer the slow part of the software. Three prototypes cost what one used to. The constraint is deciding which prototype is right.

Docking already had that shape. A job is minutes. A binding measurement is weeks or months. A faster AutoDock Vina wrapper does not change that ratio. It raises the load on the experiment. What does get cheaper inside the dry lab is trying more than one featurization, more than one docking protocol, or more than one clustering of a trajectory, and comparing them. The comparison still needs a chemist.

Who the tool amplifies

Willison cites a ThoughtWorks finding: senior and junior engineers gain the most, and mid-career engineers are the ones disrupted. Seniors know what to build and how to judge it. Juniors get a patient explainer.

The same split fits this field. Someone who knows force fields, binding free energy, RMSD versus RMSF, and why a high docking score is not a drug can now have that protocol implemented quickly. The agent does not know that the receptor is in an odd conformation, or that a crystallographic water in the site should stay. That knowledge is the job.

The role that gets thinner is running a standard pipeline without a reason to doubt it. If an agent can run the pipeline, running it is no longer the skill.

Vibe coding stops at the assay

Willison’s line is that assembling software without reading every line is acceptable when only you pay for the bugs. Other people depending on the output moves you off that line.

A wrong protonation state, an atom index off by one, or a split that leaks the test set does more than waste a queue. It points medicinal chemistry at the wrong compounds. Agents still belong in the work. The code gets the same suspicion you would give a script from a careful collaborator you have not worked with: tests, and a check of intermediate outputs against a reference set you already understand.

The question is still the expensive part

CADD could always emit a long list of candidates. Prioritizing them was always the limit. An agent does not prioritize. It lets someone who already has a view of the target, the chemical space, and the pose act on that view sooner. The inflection Willison describes is the same one arriving here. The use of it is either faster science or a faster pile of numbers.

item.title: Getting Started with Graph Neural Networks for Protein–Ligand Complexes Using DGL
item.description:
A fingerprint collapses a docked complex to a fixed vector. A graph keeps the atoms, the bonds, and the contacts, and a GNN learns from that neighborhood. is the PyTorch library this note uses. The code below is the path from an empty graph to a label. Readout and, for a set of poses, the bag come after message passing.

The rest is the DGL user-guide path, in the language of a protein–ligand complex. No prior GNN course is assumed.

Why Graphs for Molecules?

A molecule has a natural graph structure. Atoms are nodes, bonds are edges. When you extend this to a protein–ligand complex, you can add edges for non-covalent contacts (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, π-stacking) connecting ligand atoms to binding-pocket residues.

The key advantage: a GNN can aggregate information from a node’s neighborhood iteratively, so after a few layers, each atom’s representation encodes not just its own identity but the chemical context around it. This is exactly what a human medicinal chemist does mentally when reading a 2D structure.

The DGL Core: DGLGraph

Everything in DGL revolves around the DGLGraph object. Think of it as a PyTorch-native container for graph-structured data.

import dgl
import torch

# Define edges as (source_nodes, destination_nodes)
src = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 2])
dst = torch.tensor([1, 2, 2, 3])

g = dgl.graph((src, dst))
print(g)
# Graph(num_nodes=4, num_edges=4, ndata_schemes={}, edata_schemes={})

For molecular graphs, edges are usually undirected (bond A→B is the same as B→A), so use dgl.to_bidirected():

g = dgl.to_bidirected(g)

Attaching Features

Node and edge features are stored as PyTorch tensors directly on the graph:

# Node features: e.g., one-hot atomic number, partial charge, aromaticity...
g.ndata['feat'] = torch.randn(g.num_nodes(), 32)

# Edge features: e.g., bond type, interatomic distance...
g.edata['dist'] = torch.randn(g.num_edges(), 1)

This is the bridge between your cheminformatics featurization pipeline (RDKit, MDAnalysis, etc.) and the GNN. Whatever features you compute, just stick them in ndata or edata.

Heterogeneous Graphs: Protein + Ligand Together

If you want to model protein–ligand contacts explicitly (not just the ligand in isolation), DGL supports heterogeneous graphs: graphs with multiple node and edge types.

g = dgl.heterograph({
 ('ligand_atom', 'bond', 'ligand_atom'): (lig_src, lig_dst),
 ('ligand_atom', 'contacts', 'protein_residue'): (lig_ids, res_ids),
 ('protein_residue', 'contacts', 'ligand_atom'): (res_ids, lig_ids),
})

g.nodes['ligand_atom'].data['feat'] = ligand_atom_features
g.nodes['protein_residue'].data['feat'] = residue_features

This is a more faithful representation of the complex: the network can learn that certain binding-pocket residues modulate the ligand’s representation depending on how they interact.

Message Passing: How GNNs Actually Work

This is the heart of DGL and the heart of every GNN. Message passing works in two steps per layer:

Step 1: Edge-wise (messages): For each edge, compute a “message” from the source node’s features (and optionally the edge’s own features).

Step 2: Node-wise (aggregation + update): Each node collects all incoming messages, aggregates them (sum, mean, or max), and updates its own features.

Mathematically, for node v at layer t+1:

$$h_v^{(t+1)} = \psi\!\left(h_v^{(t)},\ \rho\!\left(\left\{ \phi(h_u^{(t)}, h_v^{(t)}, w_{uv}) : u \in \mathcal{N}(v) \right\}\right)\right)$$

where φ is the message function, ρ is the aggregation (e.g., mean), and ψ is the update function.

In DGL code, the fastest way uses built-in functions:

import dgl.function as fn

# Message: copy source node feature → edge mailbox
# Reduce: average all incoming messages → update node feature
g.update_all(fn.copy_u('h', 'm'), fn.mean('m', 'h'))

This runs as fused CUDA kernels, much faster than writing Python loops.

For custom behavior (e.g., distance-weighted messages):

def weighted_message(edges):
 # edges.src['h']: source node features
 # edges.data['dist']: edge distance
 return {'m': edges.src['h'] * torch.exp(-edges.data['dist'])}

g.update_all(weighted_message, fn.sum('m', 'h'))

Built-in GNN Layers

DGL ships with ready-to-use layers in dgl.nn.pytorch. The most useful for molecular tasks:

Layer When to use
GraphConv Simplest baseline, no edge features
GATConv Learns per-edge attention weights; great for contacts with varying importance
NNConv Edge-feature-conditioned messages; use when bond type or distance matters
HeteroGraphConv Wraps per-relation convolutions for heterogeneous graphs

A simple two-layer GAT:

import dgl.nn.pytorch as dglnn
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MolGNN(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim):
 super().__init__()
 self.gat1 = dglnn.GATConv(in_dim, hidden_dim, num_heads=4)
 self.gat2 = dglnn.GATConv(hidden_dim * 4, hidden_dim, num_heads=1)

 def forward(self, g, feat):
 h = F.elu(self.gat1(g, feat).flatten(1)) # (N, hidden*4)
 h = self.gat2(g, h).squeeze(1) # (N, hidden)
 return h

Graph-Level Prediction: Readout

After message passing, each node has a learned embedding. For a graph-level prediction (e.g., is this compound active?), you need to compress the variable-number of node embeddings into a single fixed-size vector. This is called readout.

DGL provides built-in readout functions:

# Mean of all node features → one vector per graph
graph_embedding = dgl.mean_nodes(g, 'h')

# Also available: dgl.sum_nodes, dgl.max_nodes

For a batch of graphs (many compounds at once):

bg = dgl.batch([g1, g2, g3, ...]) # one disconnected super-graph
# ... run message passing on bg ...
embeddings = dgl.mean_nodes(bg, 'h') # shape (batch_size, hidden_dim)

dgl.batch() is what makes mini-batch training efficient: DGL treats the batch as a single large graph (with no edges between the individual molecules), runs all convolutions in one GPU call, then recovers per-graph embeddings with readout.

The Full Graph Classification Pipeline

Putting it all together: a classifier that takes a molecule graph and outputs a binary label:

import dgl
import dgl.nn.pytorch as dglnn
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class GraphClassifier(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim, n_classes=2):
 super().__init__()
 self.conv1 = dglnn.GATConv(in_dim, hidden_dim, num_heads=4)
 self.conv2 = dglnn.GATConv(hidden_dim * 4, hidden_dim, num_heads=1)
 self.classify = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, n_classes)

 def forward(self, g, feat):
 # Message passing
 h = F.elu(self.conv1(g, feat).flatten(1))
 h = self.conv2(g, h).squeeze(1)

 # Store updated features
 with g.local_scope():
 g.ndata['h'] = h
 # Readout: mean over all atoms → graph embedding
 graph_feat = dgl.mean_nodes(g, 'h')

 return self.classify(graph_feat)


# Training loop sketch
model = GraphClassifier(in_dim=32, hidden_dim=64)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(100):
 for batched_graphs, labels in dataloader:
 feats = batched_graphs.ndata['feat']
 logits = model(batched_graphs, feats)
 loss = loss_fn(logits, labels)
 optimizer.zero_grad()
 loss.backward()
 optimizer.step()

Building a Dataset

DGL has a dataset API that handles caching processed graphs to disk, important when building graphs from PDB/SDF files is slow.

class MolDataset(dgl.data.DGLDataset):
 def __init__(self, raw_dir):
 super().__init__(name='mol_dataset', raw_dir=raw_dir)

 def process(self):
 self.graphs, self.labels = [], []
 for path in self._get_files():
 g, label = self._build_graph(path) # your featurization here
 self.graphs.append(g)
 self.labels.append(label)

 def __getitem__(self, i):
 return self.graphs[i], self.labels[i]

 def __len__(self):
 return len(self.graphs)

 def has_cache(self):
 return os.path.exists(self.save_path)

 def save(self):
 dgl.save_graphs(self.save_path, self.graphs,
 {'labels': torch.tensor(self.labels)})

 def load(self):
 self.graphs, label_dict = dgl.load_graphs(self.save_path)
 self.labels = label_dict['labels'].tolist()

Pair this with a DataLoader using dgl.dataloading.GraphDataLoader (or PyTorch’s standard DataLoader with a custom collate_fn that calls dgl.batch()).

Multiple Instances per Compound: the Bag Approach

A common scenario in ensemble docking: you dock one compound against N different receptor conformations and get N poses, each a separate graph. You want to make one prediction per compound, not one per pose.

This is a natural fit for Multiple Instance Learning (MIL). The trick with DGL:

def predict_bag(model, bag_of_graphs):
 # Stack all N pose-graphs into one batched graph
 bg = dgl.batch(bag_of_graphs)
 feats = bg.ndata['feat']

 # Run GNN - poses stay disconnected (no cross-pose edges)
 h = model.encode(bg, feats) # node embeddings

 with bg.local_scope():
 bg.ndata['h'] = h
 pose_embeds = dgl.mean_nodes(bg, 'h') # (N, h_dim) - one per pose

 # MIL aggregation over the bag
 bag_embed = pose_embeds.mean(0, keepdim=True) # mean pooling
 return model.classify(bag_embed)

The key insight: dgl.batch() keeps the poses structurally independent (no edges cross between them), so the GNN respects the fact that each pose is a separate physical structure. The MIL aggregation then decides how to combine them for the final prediction.

For a more expressive aggregation, use attention MIL:

class AttentionMIL(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, h_dim):
 super().__init__()
 self.attention = nn.Sequential(
 nn.Linear(h_dim, 64),
 nn.Tanh(),
 nn.Linear(64, 1)
 )

 def forward(self, pose_embeds): # (N, h_dim)
 scores = self.attention(pose_embeds) # (N, 1)
 weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=0)
 return (weights * pose_embeds).sum(0) # (h_dim,)

Attention MIL has a nice bonus: weights tells you which poses contributed most to the prediction, interpretable by design.

Which Chapters to Read First

If you’re using this post as a reading guide alongside the :

Priority Chapter Why
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 1.2–1.5: Graphs, features, heterograph Core data structure
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 2.1–2.2: Message passing API The computation engine
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 5.4: Graph classification Your prediction task
⭐⭐ Ch 3: GNN modules Ready-to-use layers
⭐⭐ Ch 4: Data pipeline Dataset + caching
⭐ Ch 6–8: Stochastic / distributed / mixed precision Only if dataset is huge

Summary

DGL wraps the complexity of graph-structured computation behind a clean PyTorch API. For molecular applications, the workflow is:

  1. Build a DGLGraph for each complex: atoms as nodes, bonds/contacts as edges, features from your cheminformatics toolkit
  2. Choose a GNN layer: GATConv is a strong default
  3. Run message passing: each atom aggregates information from its neighbors
  4. Apply readout (dgl.mean_nodes) to get a fixed-size graph embedding
  5. Feed into a standard MLP classifier

The library handles batching, GPU transfer, and efficient sparse operations under the hood. Once you get the featurization right, the training code looks almost identical to a standard PyTorch image classifier.

item.title: Beyond 2D Fingerprints: Encoding Protein-Ligand Interactions for Machine Learning
item.description:
A 2D fingerprint throws away the pose. Docking spent its time on contacts, hydrogen-bond geometry, and stacking, and a topology-only vector keeps none of that. Use a 2D fingerprint when the ligand alone is the object. Use a 3D interaction fingerprint when the pose is the object.

PLEC, SPLIF, and E3FP are three different objects. PLEC encodes which groups touch. SPLIF encodes the geometry of those contacts. E3FP never sees the protein.

PLEC

PLEC is an ECFP-style fingerprint of the interface. It describes the chemical neighborhood of contacting atom pairs, on both the ligand and the protein. The model sees which groups are next to which residue environments, and at what depth you asked for.

Use it when the chemistry of the contact is the signal: affinity, or reactivity at a site.

import oddt
import oddt.fingerprints as fps
from oddt.toolkits.rdk import readfile

# Load receptor and ligand
receptor = next(readfile('pdb', 'receptor.pdb'))
receptor.protein = True

ligand = next(readfile('sdf', 'docked_pose.sdf'))

# Calculate PLEC fingerprint
# depth_ligand and depth_protein control circular environment depth
plec = fps.PLEC(ligand, receptor, depth_ligand=2, depth_protein=4, size=16384)

size is the bit length. A longer vector collides less and costs more memory. 16384 is the starting point given here for ensemble docking.

If the task is reactivity at one catalytic site, a hand-built distance can be appended. The coordinate below is a placeholder.

import numpy as np
from oddt.interactions import close_contacts

# Example: compute distance from ligand centroid to a metal/active site atom
# Replace with your actual active site coordinate
active_site_coord = np.array([12.3, 45.6, 7.8])
ligand_centroid = ligand.atoms.coords.mean(axis=0)
dist_to_site = np.linalg.norm(ligand_centroid - active_site_coord)

# Append to PLEC vector
plec_extended = np.append(plec, dist_to_site)

close_contacts is imported in the original snippet and not called. The distance is a centroid-to-point norm.

SPLIF

SPLIF encodes the geometry of interacting fragments rather than a catalog of atom types. Stacking and T-shaped contacts sit in that geometry, without a hard-coded interaction list. That makes it less tied to one docking program’s interaction labels.

Use it when you want poses that reproduce the 3D binding geometry of a reference ligand.

# SPLIF is also available through ODDT
splif = fps.SPLIF(ligand, receptor, depth_ligand=1, depth_protein=1, size=4096)

The vectors are sparser than PLEC. Tanimoto similarity on them is the geometric comparison in this note.

from oddt.utils import binary_tanimoto

reference_splif = fps.SPLIF(reference_ligand, receptor)
similarity = binary_tanimoto(splif, reference_splif)
print(f"Geometric similarity to reference: {similarity:.3f}")

E3FP

E3FP is a circular fingerprint in Euclidean space. It grows out from atoms through distance, not through bonds. The same 2D structure in two conformations gets two fingerprints. The protein is absent, so this is a ligand-shape method: ligand-based screening and scaffold hopping.

# Install e3fp: pip install e3fp
from e3fp.pipeline import fprints_from_mol
from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem import AllChem

# Load mol with a 3D conformer
mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles('your_smiles_here')
mol = Chem.AddHs(mol)
AllChem.EmbedMolecule(mol, AllChem.ETKDGv3())
AllChem.MMFFOptimizeMolecule(mol)

# Generate E3FP fingerprints for all conformers
fprints = fprints_from_mol(mol, fprint_params={'bits': 4096, 'level': 5})

# Convert to dense array for ML
import numpy as np
e3fp_array = np.array(fprints[0].to_vector(sparse=False), dtype=np.float32)

For several poses, this note mean-pools the vectors.

# Mean-pool across poses - preserves pharmacophoric signal while reducing noise
fprint_arrays = [np.array(fp.to_vector(sparse=False)) for fp in fprints]
e3fp_consensus = np.mean(fprint_arrays, axis=0)

Which one

PLEC SPLIF E3FP
Sees Protein and ligand Protein and ligand Ligand only
Encodes Contact chemistry Spatial geometry Shape and pharmacophore
Ensemble noise Tolerates it well Moderate Needs aggregation
Use Reactivity, affinity Geometric screening Ligand-based screening

Across an ensemble of receptor conformations, PLEC has a frame of reference the protein supplies, so the encoding moves less when the pose jitters. E3FP has to be aggregated or the conformer noise is the feature.

None of the three is complete. The pipelines this note describes do best when a primary fingerprint is joined to a few hand-built features that the fingerprint is not learning. Profile what the model uses before you swap the whole representation.

2D fingerprints stay the right tool for a fast ligand-only screen. For a model whose question is the binding geometry, the 3D choice above is the one that matches the question.

item.title: Understanding Binding Energetics in Molecular Docking
item.description:
A docking score is a balance sheet, not a binding free energy. Polar contacts have to pay back the water they displaced. A flexible ligand pays an entropy cost. A larger ligand often scores better because it makes more contacts. Read the score only after you know which of those terms the function even has.

Desolvation

Before the ligand binds, water stabilizes its polar groups and the protein surface. Binding strips some of that water. If the protein does not replace those interactions, the cost stands.

A charged amine is the example. In water it is well solvated. Buried in a hydrophobic pocket with no partner, the lost hydration shell is unfavorable even if the shape fit looks clean.

Entropy

Binding removes motion. The ligand loses translation and rotation. A flexible ligand loses conformations. Side chains at the site often order. That entropy opposes binding.

Entropy can also help. Ordered waters released into bulk solvent are more disordered than they were in the pocket. A rigid ligand pays a smaller conformational penalty than a flexible one, which is why rigidity can improve binding efficiency.

Water that was already in the pocket

Two cases:

  • A high-energy, poorly stabilized water is a good thing to displace. It gains freedom in bulk solvent.
  • A water with strong hydrogen bonds is a bad thing to displace unless the ligand restores those bonds.

Hydration analysis is how this note suggests finding the “unhappy” waters worth targeting.

Electrostatics, and the solvent around them

Salt bridges, hydrogen bonds, and dipoles are the favorable electrostatic terms. A carboxylate next to a lysine or an arginine is the example.

The same charge is stabilized by water. Bury it without a partner and the desolvation cost can exceed the interaction you gained. The electrostatic term and the desolvation term are one argument.

Larger ligands score better

More atoms make more contacts, so many scoring functions drift toward larger molecules. Ligand efficiency (LE) divides the binding energy by the number of heavy atoms. Fit quality (FQ) is the size-adjusted efficiency named alongside it. A smaller ligand with efficient contacts can be the better lead.

What each scorer actually computes

AutoDock4 is a physics-based force field. Partial charges are explicit, commonly Gasteiger-PEOE. Electrostatics are a screened Coulomb term. Hydrogen bonding and desolvation are separate terms, calibrated on experimental binding data.

Vina is an empirical function trained on experimental complexes. It does not compute partial charges and it has no classical Coulomb term. Steric fit, hydrophobic contact, and hydrogen bonds are empirical potentials. It is faster, and the electrostatics are less visible.

Smina is a Vina fork with refined empirical potentials, a torsional penalty, and a stronger hydrophobic term. It is still empirical and still does not compute partial charges.

GNINA adds a convolutional network trained on protein–ligand complexes. The network reads the 3D pattern and does not model electrostatics as a physics term. Pose prediction is the strength named here. Detailed charge effects are the gap.

Function Electrostatics Partial charges Speed Strength named here
AutoDock4 Physics-based Explicit Slower Charged systems
Vina / Smina Empirical, implicit None Fast Large screens
GNINA Neural network None Fast Pose prediction

How to read the number

The score mixes van der Waals, electrostatics, hydrogen bonds, desolvation, and some entropy-like penalties, and several of those pieces are empirical. Use it to rank compounds in one dataset. Do not read it as an absolute affinity.

Binding is the case where the contacts, the hydrophobic fit, and the release of a bad water outweigh desolvation, the frozen ligand, and the size bias in the function you chose.

item.title: Practical System Preparation Tips for Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description:
The trajectory is already biased before the first step. The box decides how much water you pay for. The termini decide whether a fragment carries charges it never had. The frame you pick afterwards decides whether you publish an outlier.

Which box

A cubic box is orthogonal, easy to look at, and easy to debug. For a globular protein it also packs badly: the corners fill with water that the solute never touches. That is a larger system and a higher cost for the same buffer.

A truncated octahedron is closer to a sphere. For spherical solutes it cuts the solvent count by roughly 30 to 40 percent and still wraps the solute in an even shell. It is the usual compromise.

A rhombic dodecahedron leaves the least empty solvent for a given buffer. The shape is less obvious. Current MD codes handle it. The saving matters once the solute is large. This note does not give a percent for that saving.

Box Advantage Limit
Cube Simple, and natural for an elongated solute Least efficient for a globular protein
Truncated octahedron Balance of simplicity and solvent count A less obvious geometry
Rhombic dodecahedron Smallest solvent volume Least intuitive shape

When to cap the termini

A full-length chain has a real N terminus and a real C terminus. A fragment cut out of a domain does not. The cut ends are charged as if they were the ends of the protein, and they are often buried in the parent structure. That charge invents salt bridges, pulls on the fold, and shows up later as “dynamics.”

The usual caps close the backbone. ACE is the acetyl cap on the N terminus. NME is the N-methylamide cap on the C terminus.

Cap a peptide, an isolated domain, or a stretch you extracted from a larger chain. Leave the termini alone on a full-length protein whose natural ends are solvent-exposed and part of the biology.

Which frame represents the ensemble

The frame that has wandered farthest from the start is easy to notice and a poor representative. It can be one excursion.

Pool the runs. Align on a stable reference region. Measure the variation you care about: RMSD, distances between key residues, or the pocket. Cluster. Take the centroids. Those are the conformations the ensemble actually spent time in.

item.title: How to Use DataWarrior for Drug Discovery: Key Workflows From the Villoutreix Tutorials
item.description:
DataWarrior is the triage step, not the model. Bruno Villoutreix’s tutorial series is the guided tour this note follows. Part 1 is a filter: a name pattern, then a substructure, then a row list you can export.

The practice set is the Wikipedia molecule import inside the program, on the order of 22,000 structures, depending on the version. No separate download URL is given here.

What the program is

DataWarrior is a free, open-source, chemistry-aware table. Academic and commercial use are both covered. It filters in real time on text, numbers, and structure. It draws 2D and 3D plots. It calculates properties, enumerates combinatorial libraries, runs PCA and t-SNE, and can dock into a pocket. Formats are SMILES, SDF (v2 and v3), CSV, tab-delimited text, and its own DWIR project file.

A lot of the interface is a right-click, a sub-window, or a pop-up. The useful mental model is a spreadsheet that knows what a molecule is.

Villoutreix’s series is about 85 minutes across 9 videos. Part 1 is the import-and-filter path summarized here. The videos are where the clicks are. This page does not restage them as screenshots.

The Part 1 filter

Import the Wikipedia structures from inside DataWarrior. Then:

  1. Filter names with a regular expression. The examples are .*ib for kinase inhibitors, .*sartan for angiotensin receptor blockers, and .*azole for antifungals. Applied to the Wikipedia set, each suffix is a much smaller table.
  2. Draw a fragment in the structure filter. The example is a piperazine or piperidine. Rows have to match the name rule and contain the fragment. The hit atoms are shown in red.
  3. Make a row list. The example list is named cancer. Add a SMILES column. Drop columns you do not need, such as formula, molecular weight, and the structure depiction. Save tab-delimited text, cancer.txt.

Repeat with another suffix, such as .*azole, when you want a second set.

Where it sits in a project

Bring your own SDF or SMILES in, and merge assay or ADMET columns, once the Wikipedia exercise is familiar. The same two filters apply: a name or series pattern, and a scaffold. Plots are for activity, scatter, PCA or t-SNE, and the clusters you would otherwise miss in a table. The export is the clean SMILES-plus-metadata file that docking, QSAR, molecular dynamics, or a library design step can read.

Install DataWarrior from the official site, then follow the six clicks above on the Wikipedia set before you trust the same clicks on a project table. The program is the interactive layer in front of the modeling. It is not the model.

item.title: AI + Chemistry: Building Drug Discovery Pipelines with Free Tools
item.description:
An ABL kinase project can be assembled from free tools. The snippets below show the calls. They are not a trained screen: several of them run on two molecules, imatinib and a toy inactive, so they demonstrate the interface and nothing about predictive performance.

The target in the example is ABL kinase, the kinase inhibited by imatinib. Bcr-Abl drives chronic myeloid leukemia. The practical sequence is: pull measured activities, featurize, fit a model, write a 3D structure, look at it.

Data

ChEMBL is the open source of IC50 and Ki values for compounds tested against ABL. The web services or a bulk download feed a table. Pandas cleans it. NumPy does the arithmetic. This sketch starts from a CSV that is already local.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("ABL_bioactivity.csv")

RDKit

Morgan fingerprints, a Tanimoto, and a substructure check. The SMILES are imatinib and nilotinib. The SMARTS is the shared aniline–pyrimidine motif used in the example.

from rdkit import Chem, DataStructs
from rdkit.Chem import AllChem

imatinib_smiles = "Cc1ccc(cc1Nc2nccc(n2)c3cccnc3)NC(=O)c4ccc(cc4)CN5CCN(CC5)C"
nilotinib_smiles = "Cc1ccc(cc1Nc2nccc(n2)c3cccnc3)C(=O)Nc4cc(cc(c4)n5cc(nc5)C)C(F)(F)F"

mol1 = Chem.MolFromSmiles(imatinib_smiles)
mol2 = Chem.MolFromSmiles(nilotinib_smiles)

fp1 = AllChem.GetMorganFingerprintAsBitVect(mol1, radius=2, nBits=2048)
fp2 = AllChem.GetMorganFingerprintAsBitVect(mol2, radius=2, nBits=2048)

sim = DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fp1, fp2)
print(f"Tanimoto similarity: {sim:.2f}")

query = Chem.MolFromSmarts("c1ccc(cc1)Nc2nccc(n2)")
match = mol1.HasSubstructMatch(query)
print("Substructure match:", match)

DeepChem

A graph-convolution classifier on two labeled SMILES, fit for 20 epochs. That is enough to see the objects: a featurizer, a NumpyDataset, and GraphConvModel in classification mode with ROC AUC as the metric. It is not an ABL model.

import deepchem as dc
import numpy as np

smiles_list = [
 "Cc1ccc(cc1Nc2nccc(n2)c3cccnc3)NC(=O)c4ccc(cc4)CN5CCN(CC5)C", # active
 "CCOC(=O)c1ccc(cc1)N", # inactive
]
labels = np.array([1, 0])

featurizer = dc.feat.MolGraphConvFeaturizer()
X = featurizer.featurize(smiles_list)
y = labels

dataset = dc.data.NumpyDataset(X, y)

model = dc.models.GraphConvModel(
 n_tasks=1,
 mode="classification",
 metrics=[dc.metrics.Metric(dc.metrics.roc_auc_score)],
)
model.fit(dataset, nb_epoch=20)

pred_probs = model.predict(dataset)
print(pred_probs)

Open Babel

SMILES to a 3D SDF, with hydrogens.

from openbabel import pybel

smiles = "Cc1ccc(cc1Nc2nccc(n2)c3cccnc3)NC(=O)c4ccc(cc4)CN5CCN(CC5)C"
mol = pybel.readstring("smi", smiles)
mol.addh()
mol.make3D()
mol.write("sdf", "imatinib_3D.sdf", overwrite=True)

PyMOL

Load a kinase structure and the SDF. ABL_kinase.pdb is a filename, not a file this note provides.

import pymol2

with pymol2.PyMOL() as pymol:
 cmd = pymol.cmd
 cmd.load("ABL_kinase.pdb", "protein")
 cmd.load("imatinib_3D.sdf", "ligand")
 cmd.hide("everything")
 cmd.show("cartoon", "protein")
 cmd.show("sticks", "ligand")
 cmd.zoom("ligand", 5)
 cmd.png("abl_imatinib.png", width=800, height=600, ray=1)

Chemprop

Command line, then the same training call from Python. Both expect abl_activity.csv with a smiles column and an active column. Thirty epochs in the Python dict, classification mode, output directory abl_model.

chemprop_train --data_path abl_activity.csv --smiles_column smiles --target_columns active \
 --dataset_type classification --save_dir abl_model

from chemprop.train import run_training

params = {
 "data_path": "abl_activity.csv",
 "smiles_column": "smiles",
 "target_columns": ["active"],
 "dataset_type": "classification",
 "save_dir": "abl_model",
 "epochs": 30,
}
run_training(params)

A random forest on the two fingerprints

This continues from the RDKit fingerprints and the two-row labels array above. A 20% split of two rows is not a validation set. The call is here so the scikit-learn shape is visible.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = [list(map(int, fp.ToBitString())) for fp in [fp1, fp2]]
y = labels

X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100).fit(X_train, y_train)
print("Validation accuracy:", model.score(X_val, y_val))

What each tool is for

ChEMBL and PubChem hold bioactivity. RDKit handles structures. DeepChem and Chemprop are the message-passing and graph-convolution calls. Open Babel converts formats. PyMOL inspects a pose. Pandas, NumPy, and scikit-learn are the table and the baseline. All of these are free. A competitive model still depends on the table you did not sketch here: more than two compounds, a split that respects the chemistry, and a metric you compute on held-out molecules.

item.title: Interpretable Machine Learning as a Key to Understanding BBB Permeability
item.description:
A model that says “crosses” or “does not cross” is unfinished until it also says which property of the molecule pushed the decision. On a blood-brain barrier table that question is answerable, because every row already has a label and a block of chemical descriptors.

The table is B3DB, the curated set of Meng, Xi, Huang, and Ayers [1]. The 2021 paper reports 7807 compounds with a categorical BBB+ or BBB− label, and a smaller subset of 1058 compounds with a numeric logBB. This note uses the categorical extended file, which carries 1613 Mordred descriptors. The code pins one commit of that file so the columns do not drift under you. Later releases of the repository have added compounds. The paper’s count and the file you download are allowed to differ. Say which one you used.

The shell line uses a notebook shortcut. In a terminal, drop the exclamation mark. The commit hash is the pin.

wget https://github.com/theochem/B3DB/raw/87240af2b4e585d56f9681a6426af6b7f2940e96/B3DB/B3DB_classification_extended.tsv.gz

import gzip
import shutil

import pandas as pd

with gzip.open("B3DB_classification_extended.tsv.gz", "rb") as src:
 with open("B3DB_classification_extended.tsv", "wb") as dst:
 shutil.copyfileobj(src, dst)

df = pd.read_csv("B3DB_classification_extended.tsv", sep="\t")
df.head()

The label, then the descriptor block

The label column is BBB+/BBB-. Map the two strings and drop anything else, so a blank cell cannot become a positive example by falling through an else.

The Mordred columns are the 1613 fields that begin at ABC and run to the end of the table (mZagreb2 in this file). Select them by that name. A positional slice that starts at column 6 starts on the label itself, takes in identifiers and comments, and stops near VE1_Dzpe, hundreds of columns before TopoPSA. A dependence plot for TopoPSA is only meaningful if TopoPSA was one of the columns the forest saw. In this file it is column 1568, inside the Mordred block and outside that positional slice.

dropna(axis=1) then removes any descriptor that is missing for even one molecule. That is a blunt filter. One failed calculation deletes the column for the whole set. It is applied after the descriptor block has been isolated, so it cannot delete the label or shift the remaining columns into the wrong place.

label_map = {"BBB+": 1, "BBB-": 0}
df = df[df["BBB+/BBB-"].isin(label_map)].copy()
df["labels"] = df["BBB+/BBB-"].map(label_map)

descriptors = df.loc[:, "ABC":].apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
descriptors = descriptors.dropna(axis=1)
descriptors.head()

Fit on 70 percent

The split is stratified so the BBB+ and BBB− fractions match in the train and test sets. Thirty percent is held out. random_state is fixed on both the split and the forest, so a second run of this notebook hits the same rows and the same trees. The original forest call left the trees unseeded.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = descriptors.reset_index(drop=True)
y = df["labels"].reset_index(drop=True)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
 X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, shuffle=True, stratify=y
)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = rf.predict(X_test)
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))

roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, rf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
print("ROC AUC:", roc_auc)

classification_report wants the true labels first and the predictions second. The report in Figure 4 was printed with those arguments reversed, so the precision and recall it shows are exchanged relative to scikit-learn’s definition. A rerun of the code above will not match that image cell for cell.

The ROC AUC is computed from the predicted probability of the positive class. An AUC computed from the hard 0/1 predictions is a different statistic. This page does not quote a number for either, because the value belongs to the fit you just ran. Read the printout.

Which descriptors the forest used

Impurity importance is the forest’s own score: how much each descriptor reduced impurity across the trees. It favors descriptors that can split in many places. It is a reason to look, not a mechanism.

ranking = (
 pd.DataFrame({
 "features": X.columns,
 "Imp_values": rf.feature_importances_,
 })
 .sort_values("Imp_values", ascending=False)
)
ranking.head(15)

SHAP

SHAP attributes a prediction to the descriptors. The calls below match the interface in which a tree explainer returns one array per class, and index 0 is the first class. If your installed SHAP returns a single three-dimensional array instead of that list, index the class axis explicitly. Do not assume [0] still means what it meant when these figures were drawn.

pip install shap

import shap

explain = shap.Explainer(rf)
shap_values = explain.shap_values(X_test)

shap.summary_plot(shap_values, X_test)

shap.summary_plot(shap_values[0], X_test)

shap.dependence_plot("TopoPSA", shap_values[0], X_test)

Bottom line

TopoPSA came out at the top of the importance table in the run these figures record, and the dependence plot is there so that ranking can be looked at rather than quoted. Polar surface area is already a familiar constraint on CNS exposure, which makes the result plausible. It does not make it automatic. A different split, a different forest, or a descriptor block that accidentally excluded TopoPSA would have told a different story.

The useful pair is the held-out score and the attribution. The score says whether the forest separated BBB+ from BBB− on molecules it did not train on. SHAP says which descriptors carried that separation. Impurity importance is only the shortlist.

Reference

[1] Meng, F., Xi, Y., Huang, J., and Ayers, P. W. A curated diverse molecular database of blood-brain barrier permeability with chemical descriptors. Scientific Data, 2021, 8, 289.

item.title: How to build and validate 3D-QSAR models - Insights from Xu et al., 2020
item.description:
A 3D-QSAR model is a map from aligned molecular fields to a potency. The fit tells you whether that map predicts compounds you held out. The contour map tells you where changing the molecule might help. Neither result survives an alignment that put the ligands on top of one another in the wrong frame.

The workflow here is the standard CoMFA and CoMSIA stack: dock or otherwise pose the ligands, calculate fields on a shared grid, fit them with partial least squares, and refuse the model if a scrambled label looks just as good. Xu and colleagues used that stack, together with docking and molecular dynamics, on thieno[3,2-b]pyrrole-5-carboxamide inhibitors of LSD1 [1]. The field settings below are the usual ones this kind of study is built from.

Put the potency on one scale

Collect IC50 values from assays you are willing to treat as comparable. Then convert to pIC50 before any fitting:

$$ \text{pIC}_{50} = -\log_{10}(\text{IC}_{50} \text{ in mol/L}) $$

The unit is the whole conversion. An IC50 of 1000 nM is \(10^{-6}\) mol/L, so the pIC50 is 6. The same number left in nanomolar and passed to a base-10 logarithm is a different, wrong, scale. Do this conversion once, and do not mix Ki or percent inhibition into the same column without saying so.

Hold out about 20 to 25 percent of the compounds as the external test set. The training set is the remaining 75 to 80 percent. The test compounds have to sit in the same chemical space as the training compounds. A test set that is a different series is an extrapolation, and a pretty \(r^2\) on it does not mean what it says.

Alignment is the model

CoMFA and CoMSIA descriptors exist on a grid in space. Two ligands contribute to the same grid point only if you have already decided how their atoms correspond. That decision is the alignment.

A common route is to take the protein structure from the Protein Data Bank, dock the series with a program such as SYBYL or AutoDock, and align every ligand to a reference pose. Redock a ligand whose experimental pose you know. An RMSD of 2.0 Å or less between the docked pose and that experimental pose is the usual acceptance check for this workflow. It is a check on the docking setup, not a guarantee that every other ligand found the right pose.

If the reference pose is wrong, every field shifts with it. The PLS model will still quote an \(r^2\). The contours will describe the error.

Fields

CoMFA

Comparative molecular field analysis uses two fields, steric and electrostatic.

  • Grid spacing: 2.0 Å.
  • Probe: an sp³ carbon with a charge of +1.
  • Energy cutoff: 30 kcal/mol, so a clash at one grid point cannot dominate the column.

CoMSIA

Comparative molecular similarity indices analysis adds hydrophobic, hydrogen-bond donor, and hydrogen-bond acceptor fields to the steric and electrostatic ones. The attenuation factor is 0.3. It sets how fast a field falls off with distance from the atoms. Changing it changes which grid points still see the ligand.

PLS, and the numbers it produces

Partial least squares is used because the grid columns are many, collinear, and noisy. Leave-one-out cross-validation on the training set chooses the optimal number of components (ONC) and produces \(q^2\), the cross-validated \(r^2\). That is an internal number. It is not the test set.

The model is then refit on the full training set with that component count. Report:

  • \(r^2\), the fit to the training compounds.
  • SEE, the standard error of that fit.
  • The F statistic for the regression.

A training \(r^2\) far above \(q^2\) is a model that has used components the left-out compounds do not support.

Tests the model is allowed to fail

Predict pIC50 for the compounds that were held out, and compute the external predictive \(r^2\), written \(r^2_\text{pred}\).

Tropsha’s diagnostics look at that external prediction more closely than a single \(r^2\). The set includes \(r^2_0\), the slopes \(k\) and \(k'\), \(r_m^2\), and \(\Delta r_m^2\). In this workflow a model is treated as predictive when \(k\) is near 1 and \(r_m^2\) is above 0.5. Those two cuts do not replace looking at the plot of predicted against measured pIC50.

Then scramble the biological activities, rebuild, and repeat. A real relationship collapses: the randomized trials should show low \(q^2\) and low \(r^2\). If they do not, the original fit was willing to explain noise.

Reading the contours

Only after those checks do the colors become a design suggestion.

Hydrophobic and hydrogen-bond contours, when you calculated CoMSIA fields, are read the same way: a color marks a region where that property, in this alignment, moved with potency.

The numbers, in one place

Metric What it is answering
\(q^2\) Did leave-one-out on the training set still predict?
\(r^2\) How well does the final model fit the training compounds?
\(r^2_\text{pred}\) How well does it predict the compounds you held out?
SEE How large are the training residuals?
F Is the regression distinguishable from no relationship?
\(r_m^2\), \(\Delta r_m^2\) Tropsha’s closer look at the external predictions
RMSD Did the docking setup reproduce a known pose?
Y-randomization Does the fit collapse when the labels are scrambled?

Bottom line

A 3D-QSAR study is not a hunt for a large \(r^2\). It is an aligned field model that has to predict a held-out set, fail when the labels are scrambled, and only then offer a contour as a place to change the molecule. The LSD1 paper is one worked example of that order [1]. The order is the part worth copying.

Reference

[1] Xu, Y., He, Z., Liu, H., Chen, Y., Gao, Y., Zhang, S., … and Yang, M. 3D-QSAR, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation study of thieno[3,2-b]pyrrole-5-carboxamide derivatives as LSD1 inhibitors. RSC Advances, 2020, 10, 6927–6943.

item.title: Supervised vs. Unsupervised Methods in Machine Learning
item.description:
The split is not about which algorithm is fashionable. It is about whether each example already has an answer.

If the table carries a label, the task is supervised: learn the map from the other columns to that label. If it does not, the task is unsupervised: look for structure the table never names. People sometimes list a third family, reinforcement learning, where the signal is a reward collected over a sequence of actions. A static bioactivity table has no such loop. This note stays with the two tasks that table can actually support.

Read the row before you name the task

Take a chemical table with one molecule per line and columns such as molecule_chembl_id, smiles, standard_value, and class.

A row is one observation. The ChEMBL ID and the SMILES string identify that molecule. They are columns, but they are not ready-made features. A model needs numbers, and a SMILES string becomes numbers only after you compute descriptors or a fingerprint.

standard_value is already a number. If that number is what you are trying to predict, the task is regression. class is a category. In the labelling used on the acetylcholinesterase set, 1 means active and 0 means inactive. If that category is what you are trying to predict, the task is classification.

Calling every column a feature hides this. The features are the numeric columns you show the model. The label is the column you withhold. The identifier is neither.

Supervised learning

The model sees pairs: inputs, and the answer that went with them. After training, it assigns an answer to a row whose answer was hidden.

Two task types cover most bioactivity models.

  • Classification predicts a discrete label. Active or inactive, after you have defined those words with a cutoff, is classification.
  • Regression predicts a continuous value. Predicting the IC50 or the pIC50 itself, rather than a class derived from it, is regression.

The cutoff that created class is part of the supervised problem. Change the cutoff and you have changed the labels, even if every SMILES string stays the same.

Unsupervised learning

Here the model never sees an answer column. It can group rows, compress them, or estimate where the points sit densely. It cannot be “right” in the sense of matching a class you never provided.

Three techniques are the ones that show up on a chemical table.

  • Clustering groups points by similarity. On molecules, that is often a series of close analogs, or a point that sits in no series.
  • Dimensionality reduction draws a lower-dimensional map of the same rows. The map is a view of the representation you chose, not a photograph of chemical space.
  • Density estimation asks where the observations concentrate, which is also how isolated points become visible.

Association rules, known in retail as market-basket analysis, ask which items occur together in a basket. A single-molecule bioactivity table is not a basket. That method belongs to a different kind of data.

Evaluation is the uncomfortable part. With no held-out label, accuracy is the wrong word. What you can check is whether the grouping is stable under a second run or a second sample, and whether it lines up with a hypothesis you did not feed into the fit. Neither check turns the output into a supervised prediction.

Bottom line

Supervised learning requires a label on the training rows. Unsupervised learning starts without one. Classification and regression are the supervised pair. Clustering, projection, and density estimation are the unsupervised ones you will actually use on a compound table.

Choose the family from the table in front of you. If the answer column is missing, no change of algorithm will create it.

item.title: Chemical Databases Every ML Scientist Should Know for Drug Discovery
item.description:
The model is the last step. Before it, you have to decide which database actually holds the measurement you need.

Five public resources cover most of what a small-molecule project asks for. They are not substitutes. ChEMBL and BindingDB are bioactivity tables. PubChem is the broad assay archive. PDBbind pairs a bound structure with an affinity. BRENDA describes enzymes. Downloading the largest file is not the same as downloading the right one.

ChEMBL

is a manually curated set of bioactive molecules with drug-like properties, joined to the measurements reported for them. Those measurements include Ki, Kd, IC50, percent inhibition, and EC50.

That shape is what you want when the unit of analysis is “a molecule tested on a target.” Filtered well, the table becomes a screening set or a labelled file. A separate note walks through that curation for one target: search the protein, keep one activity type, collapse duplicate compounds, and only then assign a class. See .

The release notes are the place to read the current size. Quoting a compound count without saying whether it means unique structures or deposition records is how those two numbers get swapped.

BindingDB

is a public collection of measured binding affinities, mainly for proteins and small molecules. It also holds protein–protein, protein–peptide, and host–guest measurements.

A 2024 account of the database reported 2.9 million binding measurements spanning 1.3 million compounds and thousands of protein targets [1]. The first version of this note, written in 2022, described a smaller collection: more than 1.2 million measurements, more than 6,400 protein targets, and about 550,000 small molecules. Both figures are snapshots. The live site is the one to quote for a paper.

The practical entry points are searches, prepared datasets, and a similarity screen that takes an external compound set and looks for related bioactivity already in the database. Downloads have included SD files, TSV, and a database dump. Programmatic access has included a REST API, structured URLs, and KNIME. Menus move. The distinction that does not move is the content: affinities, with the target and the ligand identified.

Find My Compound’s Target

This tool takes a query molecule, finds similar compounds already in BindingDB, and returns the targets of those neighbors when they pass a similarity cutoff and an affinity cutoff. It is a neighbor search. It is not a model trained to predict a new mechanism, and a target that appears in the result is only as reliable as the neighbor and the cutoff you set.

Find Compounds for My Target

The companion search goes the other way. You name a target and ask which compounds have measurements against it. The curated rows draw on BindingDB itself and on outside sources, including ChEMBL, PubChem BioAssay, and D3R. Read the source of each row. A Ki from one database and an IC50 imported from another are not the same label.

PubChem

, at the National Center for Biotechnology Information, is the broad public archive. For a given substance it can hold chemical identity together with biochemical, pharmacological, toxicological, and other deposited description. It is free to search.

PubChem BioAssay stores the experimental records: small-molecule screens and RNAi experiments, each tied to the depositor who submitted it. Every tested substance is given an activity outcome, commonly active, inactive, or inconclusive. The depositor assigns that outcome from the assay. PubChem does not impose one potency cutoff on every record. A reported IC50, EC50, or Ki can sit beside the flag. The flag does not replace the protocol.

You can query by name, by SMILES, or by a structure you draw, and ask for an exact compound, a similar one, or a substructure. The assay page is where you go when two values disagree: the record includes the experiment, not only the number. PubChem also groups assays by protein or gene target, by assay type, by project, and by relationships such as shared active compounds.

PubChemPy

is the Python client. It covers lookup by name, substructure, and similarity, plus standardization, format conversion, depiction, and property retrieval. Use it when the next step is a table in a notebook rather than a page in the browser.

PDBbind

collects experimentally measured Kd, Ki, and IC50 values for complexes that are already in the Protein Data Bank. The useful object is the pair. A structure without an affinity, or an affinity without the complex it was measured on, answers a different question.

Basic information on each complex has been open to browse. Downloading the full contents, and some of the site’s tools, has required a free registration under a license agreement, for both academic and industrial users. Access to this resource has changed more than once since this note was first written. Check the current terms before you build a pipeline on a bulk file.

BRENDA

is an enzyme information system compiled from the primary literature. The name comes from its start in Braunschweig. It was developed for years at the University of Cologne and remains a public enzyme resource, not a compound-screening warehouse.

An entry is organized around the enzyme. It covers classification and nomenclature, the reaction and its specificity, functional and kinetic parameters, structure and stability, how the enzyme was isolated or prepared, the literature those facts came from, and cross-references to sequence or three-dimensional structure. You search it by EC number, enzyme name, organism, or a combination of those.

Academic and other non-commercial use is free. Commercial use requires a license. The project site states the current terms. BRENDA is the wrong download if the goal is a matrix of drug-like molecules and their IC50 values. It is the right one if the question is what the enzyme does and under which conditions.

Which one to open first

Ask what a row in the training file is supposed to mean.

  • A molecule tested on a target, with Ki, IC50, or a related potency: ChEMBL, then curate.
  • A binding affinity as the object of interest: BindingDB.
  • The original assay, including who decided “active”: PubChem BioAssay.
  • A 3D complex that must stay attached to its affinity: PDBbind.
  • The enzyme’s reaction, specificity, and kinetics: BRENDA.

ChEMBL, BindingDB, and PubChem can be pulled into a script. PDBbind and BRENDA are still databases you read carefully before you model anything derived from them. The script does not fix a file that answered a different question.

Reference

[1] Liu, T. et al. BindingDB in 2024: a FAIR knowledgebase of protein-small molecule binding data. Nucleic Acids Research, 2025, 53, D1633–D1644.

item.title: How to Perform Data Curation and Classify Bioactivity Data on ChEMBL Database
item.description:
A classifier does not learn activity. It learns the labels you attached to the molecules.

ChEMBL will give you the measurements. It will not give you the labels. For one target the download has many rows, often several for the same compound, some with no number, and a continuous IC50 that is not yet a class. This note turns the human acetylcholinesterase table into a file a classifier can train on: one row per molecule, a mean potency, and a class that leaves the uncertain middle out.

What the download actually contains

ChEMBL is a curated collection of bioactive, drug-like molecules and the measurements reported for them. Two counts on the release notes are easy to mix up. Compound records count depositions. Unique compounds are fewer, because the same structure can arrive from more than one source.

The ChEMBL 30 release, prepared on 22 February 2022, contained 2,786,911 compound records, 2,157,379 compounds, 1,458,215 assays, and 14,855 targets [1]. ChEMBL 33, prepared on 31 May 2023, contained 3,051,613 compound records, 2,399,743 compounds, 1,610,596 assays, and 15,398 targets [2]. A later paper describes the same platform and the kinds of data it holds [3]. Use the current release notes if you need today’s size. The curation steps below do not depend on it.

One target, one activity type

Search the target name, not a disease and not a compound, when the model is meant to describe that protein. Acetylcholinesterase returns many targets. The one used here is the human protein, CHEMBL220. Pick the organism on purpose. A homolog is a different label.

On the target report, the activity chart shows how those measurements were reported. In the interface used for this tutorial, IC50 was the common type, listed 8,205 times. That count grows as new papers are added. Treat it as a snapshot of the download, not as a property of the enzyme.

Download the IC50 slice as CSV or TSV. Then keep four columns, and delete the rest before you open the file in a notebook:

  • Molecule ChEMBL ID
  • Smiles
  • Standard Type
  • Standard Value

ChEMBL standard IC50 values are in nanomolar. If a later export renames a column, rename it back to this list. The notebook expects these headers, and it expects Standard Value to be a number.

One row per molecule

The same ChEMBL ID often appears more than once. Laboratories did not run the same assay. The values disagree, and both rows are “the” measurement until you decide on a rule.

The rule in this tutorial is a mean of Standard Value on the linear nanomolar scale, grouped by ChEMBL ID. That is a teaching choice. A factor of ten in potency is not symmetric on a linear scale, and a mean mixes assays that were not run under the same conditions. It is enough to build a labelled practice set. It is not assay-aware curation.

After the mean is attached, keep the first row for each ID and drop rows that still have a missing value. Averaging first matters: the mean has to see every replicate before the extras are deleted.

import pandas as pd

columns = ["Molecule ChEMBL ID", "Smiles", "Standard Type", "Standard Value"]
x = pd.read_csv("ache.csv")
x = x[columns]
x["Standard Value"] = pd.to_numeric(x["Standard Value"], errors="coerce")

x["mean_value"] = x.groupby("Molecule ChEMBL ID")["Standard Value"].transform("mean")
x = x.drop_duplicates("Molecule ChEMBL ID", keep="first")
x = x.dropna()

to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") turns anything that is not a number into a missing value, so a footnote or a blank cell cannot silently become text and break the mean. Restricting the frame to the four columns first stops dropna from rejecting a molecule because some unused field was empty.

The class is a gap, not a line

Potent enzyme inhibitors in this literature often sit in the nanomolar range. For a classification exercise, call a molecule active when its mean IC50 is at most 1000 nM, which is 1 µM. Call it inactive when the mean is above 10000 nM, which is 10 µM. Everything between those two cuts is left out of the file.

active = x.loc[x["mean_value"] <= 1000].copy()
inactive = x.loc[x["mean_value"] > 10000].copy()
active["Class"] = 1
inactive["Class"] = 0

combined = pd.concat([active, inactive], axis=0)
combined.to_csv("ache_labelled.csv", index=False)

.copy() matters. Assigning Class on a sliced frame is how pandas loses the new column or warns that it might. The saved file contains only the two tails. It is smaller than the curated table, and it is enriched for molecules whose mean fell clearly on one side.

What this file is

The CSV is a practice set for one target and one endpoint. A few limits travel with it.

  • The class is a cutoff on a mean, not a second experiment.
  • Replicates were averaged on a linear scale, across assays that were not matched.
  • Molecules between 1 µM and 10 µM are absent, so a model never has to make the close call.
  • The same cuts on a different target, or on Ki rather than IC50, would be a different labelling decision. Do that in a separate file.

Those choices are the model, as much as the classifier you train afterwards.
